analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal permitting for mines on public land and limits environmental review and lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 36 Republican cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing and died in committee without a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would fast-track federal review of mining projects on public land. It sets strict deadlines for environmental studies, lets agencies adopt environmental documents written by the mining company itself, shortens the window to sue over a mining permit to 120 days, and expands these rules from critical minerals to all minerals, including uranium. It would also let miners explore with up to 5 acres of surface disturbance after a 15-day notice, and let mining claim holders use public land without proving they found a valuable mineral deposit.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies and mining claim holders working federal lands, especially hardrock miners and uranium producers, who would get faster permits, weaker environmental review, fewer avenues to challenge projects in court, and expanded rights to use public land. Defense Department-backed mineral projects would also get expedited treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Sets firm deadlines for mining reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act — 12 months for an environmental assessment and 24 months for an environmental impact statement, extendable at the applicant's request [S2].
Lets the lead agency adopt an environmental impact statement or assessment prepared by or for the mining project applicant, as long as it meets NEPA requirements [S3].
Bars any lawsuit challenging a federal mining permit unless it is filed within 120 days of the permit becoming final [S2].

Expands the expedited critical-minerals process under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to all locatable minerals, not just critical ones, and directs agencies to defer to state environmental reviews [S2].
Allows mineral exploration with up to 5 acres of surface disturbance to proceed 15 days after a notice is filed, provided financial assurance is posted [S2].

Gives mining claim holders a right to occupy and conduct operations on public land with or without discovery of a valuable mineral deposit, and deems their fees to satisfy fair-market-value requirements for use of public lands [S3].
Expands the FAST-41 permitting dashboard to cover minerals production and Defense Production Act mining actions, qualifying them for expedited environmental review [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, communities near mining projects, and outdoor users of federal land. Environmental review would be compressed and partially outsourced to the applicant, lawsuits would be harder to bring, and public land could be used under the 1872 general mining law — which charges no royalties — with fees deemed to satisfy fair-market-value requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near mines and public-land users

drawbacks.text: The bill covers all locatable minerals, not just the critical minerals needed for batteries and defense, so it would loosen review for ordinary hardrock mining such as gold as well [S2].
Allowing agencies to rely on environmental documents prepared by the mining company itself raises the risk that the review reflects the applicant's framing rather than an independent analysis [S3].
A 120-day deadline to sue, combined with fixed review deadlines, makes it harder for nearby residents, tribes, and conservation groups to challenge a flawed permit before a mine is approved [S2].

Treating mining claim fees as satisfying fair-market-value requirements would let claim holders use public land cheaply, under a mining law that charges no federal royalties on hardrock minerals [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster permitting has a real purpose: mine reviews can stretch many years, and delays do slow domestic mineral supply. But this bill goes well beyond critical minerals, applies to all mining, narrows public input and lawsuits, and hands claim holders expanded rights to public land without fair-market-value payments. The speed benefits flow to a single industry while the risks — rushed reviews and weaker recourse — fall on nearby communities and the public that owns the land.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees, sent to two subcommittees, received a single subcommittee hearing in February 2023, and never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 9, 2023 by Rep. Pete Stauber with 16 original cosponsors, all Republicans [S3].
It gathered 36 cosponsors, all of them House Republicans [S4].
It was referred to the Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees and then to subcommittees on Energy and Mineral Resources and Forestry [S5].
The only further action was one subcommittee hearing on February 28, 2023; no committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action followed [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining interests are no better off, but no worse — the bill never advanced. The public retains the current, slower permitting rules with fuller environmental review and court access.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one moved; public-land safeguards remain

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Republicans, none Democrats; the bill died in committee before any vote that would have shown a partisan split [S4].

industries.note: Would get fixed permitting deadlines, expedited review for all minerals, agencies' use of company-prepared environmental documents, a 120-day window for lawsuits, and rights to use public land without proving a mineral discovery. The industry's gain comes from weaker environmental review and cheaper access to land owned by the public, under a law with no federal royalties.
The bill rewrites the critical-minerals definition so uranium is treated as a critical mineral, making uranium projects eligible for the expedited permitting process.

industries.industry: Mining claim holders on federal land
industries.note: Would gain a 'security of tenure' right to occupy and use public land with or without a proven mineral deposit, with fees deemed to satisfy fair-market-value requirements.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and conservation users of federal land
industries.note: Their interest runs with the public's: compressed environmental review, limited court access, and expanded exploration disturbance on shared public lands reduce the protections these users rely on.
